lines.L1: In twenty seventeen, Hurricane Harvey flooded Houston. Nine-one-one took seventy-five thousand calls in about three days. A normal day? Eight to nine thousand.
lines.L2: But after Superstorm Sandy, two in three people in hit communities said their neighbors helped them recover. Help is blocks away. Nothing connects it.
lines.L3: So when the oxygen battery hits ten percent, Rosa doesn't wait on hold. She opens ReliefSync, and just talks.
lines.L4: Instantly, a team of AI agents goes to work, and shows its reasoning, live. It understands the emergency, rates it life-threatening, pinpoints her address, and finds a power station nearby.
lines.L5: No black box. Every thought, tool call, and decision streams live to the people involved.
lines.L6: Now the part that makes it a marketplace. Every volunteer has an agent that knows their rating, on-time record, vehicle, battery, and price. The dispatcher sends a signal, and the agents answer with bids.
lines.L7: For life-threatening calls, there's no haggling. The best qualified, fastest responder wins, in about a second. For routine needs, agents negotiate price and quality, inside a relief-fund cap.
lines.L8: Seven factors, scored live. The winner is notified. The runners-up stay on standby.
lines.L9: Six seconds after the S.O.S., Maya's phone buzzes. No dispatcher. One tap. And everyone sees the same live route, around the flood.
lines.L10: Nine minutes later, power is restored. And Rosa's personal data? Erased.
lines.L11: ReliefSync is not a bulletin board. It's an autonomous dispatcher. Transparent. Built for broken networks. Safe by design. Disaster response runs on neighbors. We make them findable, in seconds.
lines.L12: ReliefSync. Every call for help, answered in seconds. We're applying to Y Combinator.
